title: Breviarium
author: Liberatus Carthaginensis Diaconus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1169.tmp1169.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Homiliæ quas fecit. ] Cum anLea laluissenl, editæ nunc primum sunt in secunda parte operum M. Mercatoris, et inter eas hæc ipsa cnjus meminit Socrates.
passages.english: "The homilies which he composed."] Although they had previously lain hidden, they have now been published for the first time in the second part of the works of Marius Mercator, and among them is this very one which Socrates mentions.
passages.notes: "anLea laluissenl" read as "antea latuissent" ("had previously lain hidden"). "M. Mercatoris" taken as Marius Mercator. "cnjus" read as "cujus". This appears to be an editor's note on a lemma from the text.

passages.original: Et sicut Socrates in ecclesiastica narrat Historia : < Erat quidam presbyter Antiochiæ nomine Nestorius, genere Germaniciensis , boni eloquii, quem quasi utilem ad docendum Constantinopolim principes evocaverunt. Et transactis tribus mensibus, ab Antiochia venit Nestorius, qui castitate inter plurimos praecipuus habebatur.
passages.english: And as Socrates relates in his Ecclesiastical History: "There was a certain presbyter at Antioch named Nestorius, by birth a native of Germanicia, a man of fine eloquence, whom the emperors summoned to Constantinople as being useful for teaching. And after three months had passed, Nestorius came from Antioch, a man who was regarded as outstanding among very many for his chastity.
passages.notes: The quotation from Socrates continues beyond this passage.

passages.original: Scripsit imperator sacram et beato Augustino Hipponiregiensi episcopo per Ebagnium magistrianum, ut ipse concilio praestaret sui praesentiam. Qui Ebagnius veniens Carthaginem magnam, audivit a Capreolo, ipsius urbis antistite, beatum Augustinum ex hoc mundo migrasse ad Dominum, acceptisque ab eo ad imperatorem litteris loquentibus a de obitu beati Augustini, Constantinopolim, unde venerat, rediit.
passages.english: The emperor also wrote a sacred letter to the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, through Ebagnius the *magistrianus* [an imperial courier attached to the master of offices], asking that he give the council his presence. This Ebagnius, on coming to Carthage the Great, heard from Capreolus, the bishop of that city, that the blessed Augustine had departed from this world to the Lord; and having received from him a letter to the emperor telling of the death of the blessed Augustine, he returned to Constantinople, whence he had come.
passages.notes: A stray letter 'a' before 'de obitu' is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: Eadem de re d pariter scripsit Joanni Antiocheno, Rufo Thessalonicensi, Juvenali Hierosolymitano, et Flaviano Philippensi, archiepiscopis. Scripsit et ad clernm Constantinopolitanum, admonens eos, contra doctrinam Nestorii fortiter stare, ejusque persecutiones patienter ferre, quae fructus afferrent coronarum ;
passages.english: On the same matter he likewise wrote to the archbishops John of Antioch, Rufus of Thessalonica, Juvenal of Jerusalem and Flavian of Philippi. He also wrote to the clergy of Constantinople, urging them to stand firm against the teaching of Nestorius and to bear his persecutions patiently, since these would bring the fruit of crowns;

passages.original: Et sicut Socrates dicit, cognoscens Nestorius per contentionem ad quamdam perniciem pervenisse partos, Dei genitricem Mariam vocabat, dicens : « Dicatur etiam Dei genitrix, et ea quæ fecerunt tristia c, conquiescant.
passages.english: And as Socrates says, Nestorius, recognising that the parties had come through contention to a kind of ruin, began calling Mary the Mother of God (Dei genitrix), saying: "Let her also be called Mother of God, and let the sad things that have been done be laid to rest.
passages.notes: "partos" read as "partes" ("parties"). The stray "c" after "tristia" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted.

passages.original: neque enim loqui potuit Cyrillus de epistola Ibae ad Marim, sed do aliqua alia, quam diceretur scripsisse, priusqnam rcipsa scripsisset ad Valerianum; atqui ad Valerianum scripsit anno 433, quo tempore Ibas; neque clarus vir erat, sed obscurus quidam presbyter; neque reipsa ad Marim scripserat, siquidem in epistola ad ipsum meminit lurbarum quæ occasione Diodori motæ sunt post annUm 455, quo anno Theodosius imperator sanctionem edidit de comburendis Nestorii libris; tunc enim primum de Diodoro magna contentio orta est, substitutis pro Nestorianis a factione ipsius libris.
passages.english: for Cyril could not have been speaking of the letter of Ibas to Maris, but of some other one which he was said to have written before he had actually written to Valerian; yet he wrote to Valerian in the year 433, at which time Ibas was not a famous man but an obscure priest; nor had he actually written to Maris [by then], since in the letter to him he mentions the disturbances that were stirred up on account of Diodore after the year 435, the year in which the emperor Theodosius issued the decree on burning the books of Nestorius; for it was then that the great dispute about Diodore first arose, when his books were substituted by his faction in place of the Nestorian ones.
passages.notes: The printed '455' is almost certainly an error for 435 (the year of Theodosius' edict against Nestorius' books); translated as 435. The sentence is elliptical ('quo tempore Ibas; neque clarus vir erat'), perhaps corrupt. 'lurbarum' read as 'turbarum', 'rcipsa' as 'reipsa'.

passages.original: Quibus, ut ferunt rumorcs, permotus a Cyrillus quatuor libros scripsit, tres adversus Diodorum et Theodorum, quasi Nestoriani dogmalis auctores, et alium de Incarnatione librum, in quibus continentur antiquorum Patrum incorrupla testimonia, idest, Felicis papæ Romani, Dionysii Corinthiorum episcopi, et Gregorii mirabilis Θαυματουργοῡ cognominati, Et licet in eis libris Theodori dicta laudentur contra Arianos edita, ipsum tamen magistrum Nestorii fuisse contendunt.
passages.english: Moved by these things, as the reports say, Cyril wrote four books: three against Diodore and Theodore, as the authors of the Nestorian doctrine, and another book on the Incarnation, in which are contained the uncorrupted testimonies of the ancient Fathers, that is, of Felix, pope of Rome, Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, and Gregory the Wonderful, surnamed Thaumaturgus. And although in those books the sayings of Theodore published against the Arians are praised, they nevertheless maintain that he was the teacher of Nestorius.

passages.original: Quod cognoscens Basilius, scripsit libellum, in quo docuit c libros Theodori vitandos, sicut Arii et Eu- nomii blasphemias : quod quidem prudentibus inconvenienter eum scripsisse apparet, quoniam Arius et Eunomius unam in Christo degenerem Patris substantiam praedicaverunt. Theodorus autem, ut ipsi accusant, duas e contrario docuit in Christo naturas.
passages.english: Learning of this, Basil wrote a pamphlet in which he taught that the books of Theodore were to be shunned, like the blasphemies of Arius and Eunomius. To sensible people it is evident that he wrote this inappropriately, since Arius and Eunomius preached that there was in Christ a single substance degenerate from the Father's, whereas Theodore, as his accusers themselves say, taught on the contrary that there are two natures in Christ.
passages.notes: The stray "c" before "libros" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted. "Theodore" is presumably Theodore of Mopsuestia.

passages.original: Dionysii Corinthiorum episcopi.] Addita erat in editis codicibus vox Areopagitæ, sed expungenda fuit, ipso teste Dionysie Corinthio, qui, ut est apud Eusebium, in epistolii ad Athenienses, meminit Areopagitæ Dionysii primi Atheniensium opiscopi aetate se majoris : nolim porro ego implicatum illum contentionis funem de Dionysiis cum ullo ducere, contentus venerari pareutem fidei meæ Dionysium martyrem ;
passages.english: Of Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians.] In the printed copies the word 'Areopagite' had been added, but it had to be struck out, on the testimony of Dionysius of Corinth himself, who, as is found in Eusebius, in his letter to the Athenians mentions Dionysius the Areopagite, first bishop of the Athenians, as older than himself. For my part, I would not wish to pull with anyone on that tangled rope of controversy about the Dionysii, content to venerate Dionysius the martyr, the parent of my faith;
passages.notes: Editorial note on the preceding text. Scanning errors corrected: 'Dionysie', 'epistolii', 'opiscopi', 'pareutem'.

passages.original: Quem audiens talia docentem et praedicantem Eusebius episcopus Dorylenae civitatis provinciae Phry- giie Salutariæ, cum esset orthodoxus et purus etiam amicus, prohibuit eum talia sapere et docere. Sed pertinaciter Eutyche audire nolente, retulit Eusebius causam ad Flavianum Constantinopolitanum episcopum.
passages.english: Hearing him teach and preach such things, Eusebius, bishop of the city of Dorylaeum in the province of Phrygia Salutaris, since he was orthodox and also a sincere friend, forbade him to hold and teach such things. But when Eutyches stubbornly refused to listen, Eusebius referred the case to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.
passages.notes: 'purus etiam amicus' may mean 'a sincere friend' [of Eutyches]; the phrase is slightly odd.

passages.original: Ad hæc damnavit quoque memorata synodus Eusebium episcopum Dorylæi, eo quod dixerit « duarum naturarum perfectarum Christum. »
passages.english: In addition, the said synod also condemned Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, because he had said [that] Christ [is] "of two perfect natures."

passages.original: Petagius vero occurrens.] Hinc perspicitur Pelagii cum Vigilio et Augusta conspiratio; intelligitur etiam quomodo Pelagius jam tum ageret res Vigilii, fungereturque apocrisiarii munere.
passages.english: "But Pelagius, meeting [him]."] From this the conspiracy of Pelagius with Vigilius and the Augusta is clearly seen; it is also understood how Pelagius was already at that time handling the affairs of Vigilius and discharging the office of *apocrisiarius* [papal envoy].
passages.notes: "Petagius" read as "Pelagius". "Augusta" presumably refers to the empress (Theodora). This is an editor's note on a lemma from the text.

passages.original: Sed redeunte Pelagio Constantinopolim, monachi quidam ab Hierosolymis , per quos Pelagius in Gazam transitumhabuit, venerunt cum eo ad comitatum, portantes capitula de libris Origenis excerpta, volentes agere apud imperatorem, ut Origenes damnaretur cum illis capitulis.
passages.english: But when Pelagius was returning to Constantinople, certain monks from Jerusalem, through whom Pelagius had made his passage to Gaza, came with him to the court, bringing chapters excerpted from the books of Origen, wishing to press the emperor to have Origen condemned together with those chapters.
passages.notes: 'per quos' is unclear: perhaps 'through whose [territory]' or 'by whose arrangement'.

passages.original: Fuerat ante damnatus.] Constat ex initio consequentis capitis mabgue id positum, ne scilicet Origenis damnatio post mortem præjudicium afferret adversus trium capitulorum homines, post obiium damnatos, quod nefas aiebant capitulorum patroni : Juquitur autem Liberaus de cone lio Alexandrino, quod adversus Origenem Demetrius circiter ann. 231 coegit, cujusque nemo, quod sciam, meminit ante Hieronymum; qui et ipse diversa pugnantiaque tradidit, prout aliter aliis temporibus animo affectus fuit : nam in libro de Scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, quem ante dissidium cum Rufino edidit. Demetrium dicit magna insania debacchatum in Origenem ; post dissidium, Demetrium ab Origene laceratum. Ante dissidium tradit Origenem, non propter dogmatum < novitatem, aut hæresim damnatum, quod nunc adversus eum rabidi canes simulant ; sed quia gloriam eloquentiæ ejus et scientiae ferre non poterant, et illo dicente omnes muti putabantur.
passages.english: He had been condemned before.] It is clear from the beginning of the following chapter that this was set down [here], namely so that the condemnation of Origen after death should not create a precedent against the men of the Three Chapters, condemned after their death, which the patrons of the Chapters said was impious. Liberatus is speaking of the council of Alexandria which Demetrius convened against Origen around the year 231, and which no one, as far as I know, mentions before Jerome; and he himself handed down different and conflicting things, according as he was differently disposed at different times: for in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, which he published before the quarrel with Rufinus, he says that Demetrius raged with great madness against Origen; after the quarrel, that Demetrius was savaged by Origen. Before the quarrel he reports that Origen was condemned not on account of novelty of doctrines or heresy, as rabid dogs now pretend against him, but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and learning, and when he spoke all were thought dumb.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: 'mabgue' (probably 'maxime' or 'hic', sense uncertain), 'Juquitur' = 'loquitur', 'Liberaus' = 'Liberatus', 'cone lio' = 'concilio', 'obiium' = 'obitum'.

passages.original: ] Constat aperte satis Theodoro Mopsupsteno non defuisse occasionem carpendi identidem Origenem, qui allegoriis suis omnia fere Scripturae loca corrumpebat; Theodorus enim ita litteralemsensum sequebatur, ut bac fortasse de causa Cantica canticorum interprecaretur aliquando profanius quam ut feire potuerint veteres. Verum quæ opuscula scripserit adversus Origenem, nemo in hunc usque diem explicuit, quod sciam, lateretque adhuc, nisi Hebediesu in Catalogo meminisset tomorum quinque scriptorum a Theodoro contra Allegoricos, quos haberi tradit apud Syros, sed lingua Syriaca, in quam e Graeca versi sunt.
passages.english: ] It is quite plainly established that Theodore of Mopsuestia did not lack occasion to criticise Origen again and again, since Origen corrupted almost all passages of Scripture with his allegories; for Theodore followed the literal sense so closely that perhaps for this reason he at times interpreted the Song of Songs more profanely than the ancients could bear. But what works he wrote against Origen no one, as far as I know, has explained to this day, and it would still be hidden had not Ebedjesu in his Catalogue mentioned five volumes written by Theodore against the Allegorists, which he reports are held among the Syrians, but in the Syriac language, into which they were translated from Greek.

passages.original: nam Victoris more secundus post consulatumannus is ipse est qui consulatum ὰμέσως sequitur : quare cum Basilii consulatus inciderit in annum 541, secundus post consulatum Basilii est 542, quo anno si Justinianus librum scripsit de Incarnatione adversus Acephalos, necesse est Zoilum anno 510 ordinatum fuisse ; scripsi' euim Justinianus post damnatum decreto Origenem : damnatus vero est post reversum in urbem regiam Pelagium ab ordinatione Zoili Gazæ celebrata, lectosque et diligenter ad examen vocatos monachorum Palæstinorum libellos, morasque negotio Theodori artibus injectas, quæ contingere non potuerunt, nisi idoneo temporis spatio.
passages.english: For in Victor's usage the second year after the consulship is the very year that follows the consulship immediately (amesōs). Therefore, since the consulship of Basilius fell in the year 541, the second [year] after the consulship of Basilius is 542. If Justinian wrote the book on the Incarnation against the Acephali in that year, Zoilus must necessarily have been ordained in the year 540. For Justinian wrote after Origen had been condemned by decree; and he was condemned after Pelagius had returned to the imperial city from the ordination of Zoilus held at Gaza, after the petitions of the Palestinian monks had been read and carefully brought to examination, and after the delays introduced into the business by the contrivances of Theodore. These things could not have happened except over a suitable span of time.
passages.notes: The text reads 'anno 510' for Zoilus' ordination. This is very likely a misprint for 540, given the argument (541 and 542 for Basilius' consulship and its second post-consular year) and the competing dates of 544 and 545 cited in the preceding context. I have translated 540. Scanning errors corrected: 'consulatumannus' read as 'consulatum annus'; "scripsi' euim" read as 'scripsit enim'. 'ὰμέσως' is Greek ἀμέσως, 'immediately'. Theodore is presumably Theodore Ascidas, though the text does not say so. 'Victoris more' is taken as 'in Victor's manner of reckoning', i.e. the usage of the chronicler Victor of Tunnuna.
